Their infatuation with seed oils is the epitome of this. Extensive onboarding, forced to free trial. The onboarding experience creates unnecessary friction for a product that’s supposed to offer a free trial. Even though billing runs through Apple subscriptions (so you’re not directly entering payment details), users still have to subscribe upfront before they’ve had a real chance to explore the product.

The predictable outcome is that many people myself included immediately cancel the subscription after signing up so they don’t risk being charged later. Once a user has already canceled, the likelihood of them returning to renew is much lower, which ultimately works against long-term adoption.

A better customer experience would allow users to try a limited version of the product first, demonstrate value quickly, and then ask for a subscription after they’ve decided it’s worth keeping. Strong products retain customers through value, not by creating cancellation risk or onboarding fatigue.

I also noticed inconsistencies and what seems like bias in their scoring. If you’re hoping the app tests or provides information about things like heavy metals, it does not. I haven’t seen a single product with heavy metal testing data attached, which was one of the reasons I wanted to try it.

Another inconvenience: when they suggest healthier alternatives, there are no links to purchase the items. You have to leave the app, Google every product yourself, and hunt down where to buy it. As a busy mom of four, that completely defeats the purpose of having a “convenience” app.

I should have read the reviews first, and that’s on me but hopefully this helps someone else. At this time, I cannot recommend the Olive app.
